planting.note: Plant grafted, dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring into deep, well-drained soil, well away from vegetable beds and other juglone-sensitive plantings.

directions: Kwik-Krop is a long-circulated named black walnut selection prized chiefly for its precocity, beginning to set nuts within about six years of grafting, well ahead of most seedling trees and many other named cultivars that take a decade or more to reach bearing age. It has been used alongside cultivars such as Emma K and Sparks 127 in University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry flavor and quality evaluations of grafted black walnut selections. Plant it in deep, well-drained loam in full sun with generous room to mature into a large shade tree, and pair it with a second black walnut cultivar nearby to improve nut set through cross-pollination. Like all black walnuts, its roots, hulls, and leaf litter exude juglone, so keep tomatoes, apples, and other juglone-sensitive species well outside the eventual dripline.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted, dormant trees in late winter to early spring into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from juglone-sensitive garden plants.

directions: Sparks 127 was selected from a tree found by Archie Sparks in Iowa and is distinguished by a spur-type fruiting habit, in which nuts cluster on short lateral spurs rather than spreading along the full length of the shoot, a trait linked to earlier and heavier bearing than typical seedling black walnuts. It has become a benchmark cultivar in University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry black walnut variety trials and flavor studies, often evaluated alongside Emma K and Kwik-Krop. Give it deep, well-drained soil in full sun with wide spacing to accommodate its eventual size as a shade tree, and plant a second cultivar nearby since black walnut sets larger crops with cross-pollination. Keep tomatoes, peppers, and other juglone-sensitive plants well outside the mature dripline, as the roots and hulls release the growth-inhibiting compound juglone.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: Willamette Chestnut (Blight-Resistant American-Chinese Hybrid, Large-Nutted Southern Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; give it another chestnut cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and heavier crops.

directions: Willamette was bred in North Carolina in 1953 by crossing a blight-tolerant native American chestnut seedling from Ohio with a composite Chinese chestnut parent combining the Kuling, Meiling, and Nanking selections, giving it strong genetic resistance to chestnut blight along with much larger nuts than a typical Chinese chestnut. The medium-sized, upright, widely spreading tree flowers late and profusely after full leaf-out, which helps it dodge late spring frosts, and bears heavy, regular crops of extremely large, glossy chocolate-brown nuts that are notably sweet and release freely from the burs at ripening in mid-September. It has long been favored for orchard and food-forest plantings in the southeastern United States, where it tolerates summer heat and humidity better than European or American chestnut. Give it deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and mulch to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity through the growing season.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP7,195 — Willamette Chestnut

common_name: Oz Hunter Ozark Chinquapin (Precocious Blight-Resistant Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in well-drained, acidic, rocky to loamy soil in full sun; plant a second Ozark chinquapin nearby for cross-pollination and a fuller nut set.

directions: Oz Hunter is a patented Ozark chinquapin selection produced from a controlled cross of two blight-tolerant parent trees from Missouri and Arkansas research plots, chosen for outstanding precocity and heavy, dependable annual crops. Burs typically hold one to six small, sweet, high-protein nuts, and it grows notably faster than wild Ozark chinquapin seedlings even without fertilizer or soil amendment, reaching bearing age well ahead of typical wild stands decimated by chestnut blight. Nut drop begins in early-to-mid September and continues over several weeks, so plan on repeated ground collection through the harvest window. Site it on the same dry, rocky, acidic, well-drained ground favored by wild Ozark chinquapin, since it does not tolerate wet or heavy clay soils.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP33,246 — Ozark chestnut tree named 'Oz Hunter'

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raritan needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar such as Monmouth or Somerset nearby for a full nut set.

directions: Raritan is a vigorous, upright hazelnut released in 2020 by Rutgers University, one of the first cultivars bred specifically to combine strong quantitative resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight with high yields under Mid-Atlantic growing conditions, where the disease had long prevented commercial European hazelnut production outside the Pacific Northwest. It produces medium, round, well-blanching kernels and ripens early, typically ready to harvest in the first to second week of September. Because it is self-incompatible, plant it with a genetically compatible pollenizer such as Monmouth or Somerset, sited so their bloom periods overlap. It performs best in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil within its recommended zone 6-7 range, reflecting its breeding and testing focus on New Jersey and the broader Mid-Atlantic region.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station — E368: Choosing Plants for a Hazelnut Orchard in New Jersey
U.S. Plant Patent PP32,460 — Corylus plant named 'Raritan'

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Monmouth needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar such as Raritan or Somerset nearby for a full nut set.

directions: Monmouth is a moderately vigorous, slightly spreading hazelnut released in 2020 by Rutgers University as part of the first wave of Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant cultivars bred for Mid-Atlantic growing conditions. It is a high-yielding, early-blooming selection producing medium, round kernels that blanch very well after roasting, making it well suited to confectionery use as well as fresh eating. Because it is self-incompatible, pair it with a compatible pollenizer such as Raritan or Somerset for consistent nut set, and harvest in the first to second week of September when nuts drop free of the husk. It is recommended for USDA zones 6-7, reflecting its New Jersey breeding and trial origins.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station — E368: Choosing Plants for a Hazelnut Orchard in New Jersey
U.S. Plant Patent PP32,462 — Corylus plant named 'Monmouth'

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hunterdon needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar nearby for a full nut set.

directions: Hunterdon is a vigorous, upright hazelnut with a slightly spreading habit, one of four cultivars released by Rutgers University in 2020 for Eastern Filbert Blight resistance and productivity under Mid-Atlantic conditions. It carries a high level of blight tolerance, though somewhat less than sibling cultivars Raritan and Monmouth, and is prized for mostly round, medium-to-large kernels with outstanding flavor and excellent blanching. It is self-incompatible and among the earliest of the Rutgers releases to ripen, typically ready from late August into the first week of September. Grow it in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil within its recommended zone 6-7 range, and plant a compatible pollenizer for dependable annual crops.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station — E368: Choosing Plants for a Hazelnut Orchard in New Jersey
U.S. Plant Patent PP32,461 — Corylus plant named 'Hunterdon'

common_name: Somerset Hazelnut (Rutgers EFB-Resistant Compact Eastern Filbert)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Somerset needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar such as Raritan or Monmouth nearby for a full nut set.

directions: Somerset is the most compact of the four Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant hazelnut cultivars released by Rutgers University in 2020, reaching only about two-thirds the size of its sibling Raritan at maturity, which makes it a good fit for smaller home orchards. Its resistance comes from a distinct vertical resistance gene inherited from the European hazelnut 'Ratoli' and has held up with no observed blight in Rutgers field trials. It is a reliably heavy bearer even on young trees, producing small-to-medium, round kernels with an excellent kernel percentage and good blanching, harvested in the first to second week of September. Being self-incompatible, plant it with a compatible pollenizer such as Raritan or Monmouth, and grow it in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil within its recommended zone 6-7 range.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station — E368: Choosing Plants for a Hazelnut Orchard in New Jersey
U.S. Plant Patent PP32,494 — Corylus plant named 'Somerset'
